questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The sentence-final particle in a request
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a question from an announcement, a suggestion and a complaint
questions.stem: A colleague has sent a message about a deadline and a learner has to reply without accusing anybody. Which reply asks a question rather than announcing a conclusion?

options.text: 这个是不是下周三就要交？您确认一下，我怕记错了。
这个下周三就要交了，您确认一下，我怕记错了。
options.misconception: removes the question and leaves a date as a fact, so the reply confirms rather than asks

options.text: 这个下周三要不要交？您确认一下，我怕记错了。
options.misconception: asks whether the colleague is going to hand something in rather than asking when the deadline falls

options.text: 这个下周三才交呢，您确认一下，我怕记错了。
options.misconception: marks a contrast and the sentence-final particle turns the whole line into a complaint about the timing

questions.explanation: The difference between a question and an announcement in Chinese is frequently a particle, and that is why a learner can write a sentence that sounds like a question to a speaker and reads to them as a statement. 是不是 at the front and 吗 at the end together make a yes-no question out of what is otherwise the same order of words, and that is the device the keyed sentence relies on. B has the identical content and no question in it, so a colleague reads a correction and may reasonably feel it. C does use a question form, but the question it asks is a different one: 不要 here pairs with the action of handing in, so the colleague is being asked whether they intend to do it rather than when it is due, and that misreading will delay the answer. D is the one to be careful with, because 呢 looks like it is asking for information and is in fact doing something else entirely. Paired with 才, it marks a contrast between an expectation and the fact, which makes the whole line a complaint, and a complaint delivered with a polite particle is still a complaint.
questions.hint: Ask which particle makes it a question, and check what the words in front of it are actually asking about.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Refusals that keep a relationship available
questions.learningObjective: screen refusals for the ones a colleague can hear and answer
questions.stem: A learner has to turn down several invitations from colleagues and wants to keep each relationship open. Four of the five replies below decline in a form that does that. Which four?

options.text: 下个月我这边正好有一个项目要收尾，实在走不开，所以这次我就不去了。
我没时间去，对不起，就这样吧。
options.misconception: gives the reason and then closes the exchange, so the inviter has nothing to respond to and cannot retry later

options.text: 我看一下时间再答复您，可以吗？
我最近有点忙，这周恐怕不行，下次一定来。
我不能去，我不喜欢这种活动，你们自己玩吧。
options.misconception: adds a dislike of the activity itself, which passes a verdict on the inviter's choice rather than on the speaker's calendar

questions.explanation: Three of these decline and leave something behind for the other person, and the thing they leave behind is the same in all three: a way to ask again. A supplies an impersonal reason and a definite no, which is what makes it usable, since an indefinite refusal is harder to plan around. C does not refuse at all, it postpones, and it asks permission to do so, which leaves the inviter in charge of what happens next. D combines a soft limit with an opening, and the 恐怕 is doing the softening rather than a 吗, so the sentence stays a statement while the politeness sits inside it. The two rejected replies share a structure worth naming. B apologises and then ends the conversation with a phrase that has no addressee inside it, so the inviter is left with a social task they cannot perform. E is the more damaging of the two, because the second clause is a comment on the activity and therefore on the person who proposed it, and that will cost the speaker the next invitation as well as this one.
questions.hint: Ask of each reply whether the inviter is left with a way to ask again, and what the last clause of it is about.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Why a question form is a polite request
questions.learningObjective: explain to a learner what a question form changes about a request in Chinese
questions.stem: A learner writes 麻烦你把文件发我 to a colleague and asks why several speakers she recorded said the same request as a question instead. Explain what the question form changes about the exchange, and what it costs the speaker to use it.

answer.exemplar: What the question form changes is the position of the other person, and that is the whole of it. An order in this language is understood as a statement about what will happen: the speaker has decided and is reporting the decision, and the listener's part in it is to carry it out. A question about the same act makes no such statement. The speaker is asking what the listener intends to do, and the listener is therefore the one holding the answer, which means the listener can give a different one. That single shift is what a learner is buying by turning a statement into a question, and it is worth naming as buying rather than adding, because the politeness is not an extra courtesy on top of the request. It is a different shape for the same content. It is also why the question form is available where an English request might simply be a request, and why a learner who records several native speakers will hear it so often: the mechanism is available at no cost, since a question costs the same to say as a statement. The cost is real and a learner should be told about it, because a habit of asking questions has a price. Repeated questions of this kind transfer a share of the work of deciding to the listener, and a colleague who has answered four of them begins to feel that the speaker is managing the colleague rather than asking a favour. There is also a cost in clarity, since a question can be answered with a maybe, and a maybe is difficult to plan around. So the rule to teach is not to ask instead of ordering, but to ask when the other person has a genuine interest in the answer. A manager who might say no has one. A colleague who has no reason to refuse does not, and there the statement is the better tool, because it is the only one of the two that gets a definite answer.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked as correct for locating the change in the position of the listener rather than in the tone, for giving a cost rather than only a benefit, and for deriving a rule about when the question form is worth using rather than a blanket preference for it.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the answer after the sentence is spoken, and what happens if the same request is asked for the fifth time this week.
